oneSentence: A set of coded instructions that tells a computer how to take input, process it and produce output.
plainExplanation:
Software is the part of a digital system that tells the hardware what to do. Hardware is the physical machine: the screen, processor, keyboard, storage and network equipment. Software is the coded instructions and rules those parts follow.

Something goes in, such as text, numbers, clicks, images or data from another system. The software applies steps to that input. Those steps might be simple, like sorting names, or more complex, like checking for duplicate records or generating draft text.

Then something comes out. The output might be a message on screen, a saved file, a warning, a chart or an action in another system. If the software has a fault, often called a bug, the output may be wrong even when the computer itself is working normally.

Software is a broad term. An algorithm is a method or procedure; software is the full working implementation of one or more methods in code. A model, in AI, is usually one component inside software, not the whole application. So not all software uses AI, and not all parts of AI systems are models.

everydayAnalogy.title: A registry office checklist and clerk
everydayAnalogy.story: In a city registry office, a clerk receives forms from many counters. The office manager gives the clerk a written checklist: read the name, compare birth dates, flag possible duplicates and place each form in the correct tray. The same desk and trays stay the same, but the checklist can be updated when the office changes its procedure. At the end, the office produces a clean list and a small stack of records that need human review.

mapping.analogyElement: sorting into trays and flagging duplicates

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A clerk can use judgement, ask questions and handle unusual cases in flexible ways. Ordinary software does only what its coded instructions and connected components allow. Also, real software can run millions of steps per second and may include many modules, which a single office checklist does not show.

visual.title: How software turns input into output
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, a reader should be able to explain that software sits between input and output, applying coded instructions on hardware.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram with four boxes connected by arrows. Read from input to output. The second box names software as instructions, and the third shows processing actions such as checking, sorting and calculating. Small labels below show that hardware runs the software but is not the same thing.

steps.label: Input arrives
steps.explanation: Data or user actions enter the system, such as typed names, button clicks or uploaded files.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box labelled 'Input' with icons for text, numbers and a mouse click. Add example caption: 'registry records'.

steps.label: Software gives instructions
steps.explanation: The program contains coded rules telling the computer what steps to perform.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box labelled 'Software' with stacked lines representing code. Add a small note underneath: 'instructions, not the machine itself'.

steps.label: Processing happens
steps.explanation: The software checks, sorts, compares, calculates or transforms the input.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box labelled 'Processing' with three small tags inside: 'check', 'compare', 'sort'. Show arrows moving through the tags.

steps.label: Output appears
steps.explanation: The system returns a result, such as a report, alert, saved record or updated screen.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box labelled 'Output' with icons for a report, warning sign and saved file. Add a side note: 'may still need human review'.

visual.interaction: Hovering or tapping each box reveals one sentence with an example: input record, coded rule, duplicate check, flagged result.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram is a four-step flow from left to right. First, input enters the system as text, numbers or clicks. Second, software is shown as coded instructions that tell the computer what to do. Third, processing applies those instructions to check, compare, sort or calculate. Fourth, output appears as a report, alert or saved file. A note explains that hardware runs the software, but hardware and software are different parts of the system.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-box flow replaces any animation. Arrows show the same sequence: Input, Software, Processing, Output, with the same labels and notes visible at once.

workedExample.scenario: A local registry system helps staff find possible duplicate person records.
workedExample.input: Three records: 'Amina Yusuf, 12 May 1998'; 'Amina Yousuf, 12/05/1998'; 'Amina Yusuf, 3 March 2001'.
process: The software receives the three records from the database.
It standardises the date format and ignores small spelling differences it was coded to treat as similar.
It compares names and birth dates across the records.
It flags the first two as a possible duplicate pair and leaves the third record unflagged.
workedExample.result: The output is a review list with one possible duplicate pair for a staff member to check, not an automatic deletion.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN team reviews programme monitoring data and uses approved internal software to combine monthly spreadsheets, check for missing values and produce a dashboard for managers.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: This shows that software often handles routine data tasks before any AI feature is involved, and that the output supports human review rather than replacing it.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not upload confidential, personal or protection-sensitive programme data to an unapproved public AI service or other unapproved software tool.

whyItMatters:
Non-specialists hear many digital terms used as if they mean the same thing. Knowing what software is helps you ask better questions: What data goes in? What steps are applied? What output comes out? Is the problem in the hardware, the software, the data or the human process around it?

This matters for procurement, risk, accountability and everyday use. A vendor may describe a product as AI when it is mostly ordinary software with fixed rules. A useful discussion depends on separating the overall application from one algorithm or one model inside it. That helps people judge reliability, privacy, cost, maintenance needs and where human oversight is required.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Software means the same thing as AI.
commonMisconceptions.correction: AI is only one subset of software. Many programs follow fixed rules and do not learn from data. Calling all software AI can hide what the system actually does and what risks it creates.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If software gives a result, the result must be correct.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Software can fail because of coding bugs, poor design, wrong settings or bad input data. A computer can follow instructions exactly and still produce an unhelpful or incorrect output if the instructions or data are flawed.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: An algorithm and software are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: An algorithm is a method for solving a problem, like a procedure on paper. Software is the implemented code, interface, error handling, connections and other parts needed to run that method on a real machine.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Software is the set of instructions that makes a computer or phone do useful tasks, from showing a webpage to checking records.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Software is executable code and related components that run on hardware to perform specified operations on inputs and produce outputs. In practice, it often includes program logic, user interface elements, configuration files, libraries, database queries, network calls and error handling. One software application may contain many algorithms and, in some systems, one or more AI models. That is why software is broader than an algorithm and broader than a model. The same hardware can run different software, and changing the software can change the system's behaviour without changing the physical machine.

keyTakeaway: Software is the broad set of coded instructions that runs on hardware; an algorithm or AI model may be part of it, but neither term means the whole thing.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best describes software?
options: Only programs that use artificial intelligence
The physical parts of a computer, such as chips and screens
Coded instructions that tell a computer how to process input and produce output
A dataset used to train a machine-learning model
quickCheck.explanation: Software is the instructions layer. Hardware is the physical machine, data is the input material, and AI software is only one subset of all software.

contested: The core idea of software is not very disputed, but the boundary between ordinary software and AI software is often debated, especially in marketing and policy discussions.

issues.problem: This definition is almost indistinguishable from the page's definition of an algorithm. Adding only that the instructions are coded does not explain that software is the implementation that runs on hardware and may contain algorithms, models and supporting components.
issues.fix: Code and related components that run on hardware, often implementing algorithms to process input and produce output.

issues.problem: “AI is only one subset of software” contradicts the supplied definition of AI as a set of computer methods. AI methods can be implemented in software, but the methods are not themselves a subset of software. The reference to programs that follow fixed rules and do not learn also misleadingly suggests that learning from data separates AI from non-AI, although some AI methods use fixed rules.
issues.fix: AI methods can be implemented in software, but AI and software are not the same category. Many programs do not use AI methods. Calling all software AI can hide what the system actually does and what risks it creates.

issues.problem: The analogy does not map its key executing agent. The clerk follows the checklist, so the clerk corresponds most closely to processing hardware, while the mapping assigns hardware only to the passive desk and trays. This obscures how software is executed.
issues.fix: A clerk can use judgement, ask questions and handle unusual cases flexibly, while software is executed by hardware within its coded and connected capabilities. Here, the clerk represents the processor; the desk and trays represent supporting hardware. Real software may also contain many interacting modules.

issues.problem: The four-box sequence presents “Software” and “Processing” as consecutive stages. Processing is what occurs when hardware executes the software, not a separate stage after software. The diagram therefore weakens the mechanism stated in its learning objective.
issues.fix: Use three boxes: Input, Software processing on hardware, and Output. Show checking, comparing and sorting inside the middle box. Update the accessibility and reduced-motion descriptions to match.
